title: Spec-Driven Development: Specs as the Durable Contract — Audio Guide

chapters.title: The Control System Model
chapters.script: Spec-driven development is the professional response to the chaos of unsupervised code generation. Instead of prompting an agent to create a button and then iterating against whatever it produces, you decouple the specification, the what and the why, from the implementation, the how. The specification becomes a permanent technical artifact and a contract, between humans, and between humans and the agent. The mental model is a control system with a small, durable setpoint driving a large, disposable output. Vibe coding is open loop. A high-level prompt produces code, you eyeball it, you correct the agent in a long conversation whose history is never saved, and technical debt mounts because nothing authoritative records what was intended. Spec-driven development closes the loop by promoting intent to a versioned file. A few sentences in a specification, use a lightweight database with a typed object mapper, amplify into hundreds of lines of implementation. Change one sentence to a different database and the same amplification regenerates downstream. Because the setpoint is tiny relative to the output, the cost of supervising an ultra-fast coding agent collapses from read every line of difference, to review the specification, then spot-check the amplification. This is why the specification, not the code, is the primary engineering artifact. It has the highest leverage-to-size ratio in the system, it survives across agent sessions, and it is the only place where human architectural judgment is recorded once and reused indefinitely. The agent is a stateless amplifier. The specification is the memory.

chapters.title: Why Specs Beat Vibes
chapters.script: Vibe coding is fast for a button and catastrophic for a project. You write a prompt, hope for the best, point out what is wrong, and repeat. The result is disposable code and an unsaved dialogue. There is no artifact a teammate, or a future agent session, can read to learn what the system is supposed to do. Spec-driven development trades a small amount of upfront writing for three compounding benefits. The first is leverage. Large code changes are controlled by small specification changes, so one clause about look and feel can translate to hundreds of lines of styling, and editing the specification is dramatically more efficient than editing code by hand. The second is context durability. Specifications eliminate context decay between sessions. Agents are stateless. Every session boots fresh, so the highest-quality context must be loaded at boot time, and a specification is exactly that durable boot payload. This is the same discipline as context engineering, where you decide what the model must know the instant it starts. The third is intent fidelity. When you define the problem, the success criteria, and the constraints precisely, the agent can elaborate a fuller plan that matches what you actually need rather than what a terse prompt implied. One effective technique is to converse with an agent to make the key architectural trade-offs using your own judgment, then have the agent summarize the agreed decisions back into the specification.

chapters.title: The Project Constitution
chapters.script: Before any feature, spec-driven development establishes a constitution, the project-level decisions formalized into three living documents. The first states the mission, the vision, the audience, and the scope. The second states the technology stack, the shared understanding of development and deployment technologies and their constraints. The third is a roadmap, a phased sequence of features that evolves over time. A constitution is agent-agnostic and more structured than a single top-level rules file, and it captures the agreement on key decisions both between the human and the agent, and between humans on the team. You do not write the constitution alone. You write it in conversation with the agent, which surfaces architecture patterns you had not considered, existing packages that already do the work, and trade-offs such as speed versus data fidelity. Architecturally this is identical to the discipline of system prompting. The constitution is the highest-priority, lowest-trust-required instruction set that constrains everything the agent generates afterward. It is the codebase's constitution in the same sense that a system prompt is an application's constitution, durable, authoritative, and the first thing loaded.

chapters.title: The Per Feature Loop
chapters.script: Once the constitution exists, every feature runs through a repeatable loop. You specify, then plan, then implement, then validate. The key skill is choosing the right level of detail. Treat the agent as a highly capable pair programmer. Give it rich context about goals, mission, audience, and constraints, and less about the low-level decisions it can figure out itself. You start each feature with fresh agent context on a dedicated branch. The agent draws what it needs from the authoritative source, the constitution, then helps produce a feature specification, a task plan, collected requirements, and a validation scorecard. The agent asks clarifying questions. You make the key decisions, pin the framework version, enforce strict typing, choose plain database migrations, and you watch for conflicts. After implementation you flush the context and review against the specification, focusing on whether the feature works and reflects the specification rather than on which styling classes were used. A mistake in the code usually traces back to a mistake in the plan, so you correct both the specification and the implementation to keep requirements and validation in sync. For areas where small mistakes compound, security, database migrations, you run task groups one at a time instead of implementing the whole plan in a single step. The validation scorecard turns the vague question, does this look right, into a checkable contract.

chapters.title: Replanning And Legacy Work
chapters.script: Between features you deliberately run slow to run fast. The constitution is a living document. When you discover a missing testing preference, or the product manager reports that forty percent of users are on mobile and you must emphasize responsive design, you make the change on a dedicated replanning branch so you can track which version of the constitution produced which code. You then instruct the agent to update existing feature specifications and implementations to reflect the constitutional change, so specification and code evolve together, never independently. The most aggressive move is the minimum viable product gamble, a controlled stress test. It is a variation of the standard prompt that tells the agent to implement the rest of the roadmap at once, with guidance about existing specifications. You only take this risk when you are confident in the quality of your constitution and specifications and can handle the review load. If the result diverges from intent, that divergence is diagnostic feedback on your context quality, not just a bug. Spec-driven development is not only for greenfield work. To bring it to a legacy project, you start a fresh agent session on the main branch without a specifications folder and run the constitution step against existing artifacts, a readme, a to-do file, issue trackers, spreadsheets. The agent explores the codebase through tool calls and reverse-engineers the artifacts, extracting the file structure, the framework versions, and the roadmap items from what already exists. The constitution then aligns future agent changes with what past developers already built.

chapters.title: How Agents Actually Run
chapters.script: Understanding why spec-driven development works requires looking at how a coding agent actually runs. An agent is stateless across sessions. Each invocation boots with an empty working memory and a finite context budget. There is no persistence of the previous dialogue unless something external recorded it, which is precisely the failure mode of vibe coding. Spec-driven development treats the specification set as the agent's externalized memory. At boot, the constitution and the active feature specification are loaded as the highest-quality context, so the model's limited budget is spent on the next unit of work rather than on reconstructing forgotten intent. Between phases you deliberately flush the context window, ensuring the next feature is driven by the written specification, the intent, and not by a stale memory snapshot of the last conversation. Versioning is the other half of the runtime. Because specifications and code live in version control, a replanning branch records exactly which constitution version produced which implementation, so a regression can be traced to a constitutional change rather than guessed at. The agent discovers artifacts at runtime through tool calls, reading files and exploring directories, which is why good repository hygiene matters. The specification is only authoritative if the agent can reliably find and read it. This model, boot context plus versioned artifacts, is what converts a fast but forgetful generator into a supervised, auditable engineering process.

chapters.title: Build Your Own Workflow
chapters.script: Once the loop is mastered, the repeated prompting, write these files, plan, implement, validate, is friction worth automating. You automate it with an agent skill, an open-standard, reusable capability authored with the agent's own skill creator. Skills can be per-project or global, and they are invoked through progressive disclosure. The agent reads a skill's description and decides when to call it. Because that judgment degrades as the context window grows, apply the same heuristic as explicit file tagging. If you know you want a skill used, name it explicitly to save thinking tokens. This is the automation pattern of capturing a repeatable engineering process as a first-class, named artifact. The final principle is agent replaceability. Models and agents improve every month, so you do not want a workflow welded to one vendor. Open standards make agents swappable while the workflow and tools stay put. There is a protocol for connecting external tools, a conventional rules file for agent instructions, agent skills for repeatable workflows plus context, and a client protocol for connecting agents to editors. A feature-specification skill authored for one agent runs unchanged in another once copied to its path. Spec-driven development moves the work from the how to the what and the why, so the how, meaning which specific agent executes the specification, becomes an interchangeable implementation detail. The specifications you write today become the memory of your projects tomorrow. Keep them sharp, and the agent stays a replaceable driver of an engineering process you own.

chapters.title: The Tool Landscape
chapters.script: The course teaches one workflow, but spec-driven development is a label several tools wear differently. It is not just one thing. Three tools are worth knowing because they bracket the design space. The first is the lightweight end, an editor-based tool with a fixed flow of requirements, then design, then tasks, one document per step, requirements expressed as user stories with given, when, and then acceptance criteria, and a flexible memory bank it calls steering. The second is the most customizable, a command-line tool that scaffolds workspace files for many coding assistants, driven through slash commands, whose memory bank is the constitution itself, immutable high-level principles applied to every change, with heavy interpreted checklists acting as a per-step definition of done. The third is the only one explicitly chasing the deep end, a framework in private beta that doubles as a tool server, where code files carry a generated-from-specification header, a command reverse-engineers a specification from existing code, tags pin the exposed interface, and a build command regenerates the file. The decisive axes that separate them are workflow opinionation, how many artifacts a single specification sprawls into, whether a memory bank is optional or mandatory, and the abstraction level the specification sits at. Pick the tool by problem shape, not by brand.

chapters.title: A Maturity Taxonomy
chapters.script: The most useful contribution from the skeptical literature is a maturity ladder that cuts through the marketing. At the first rung, spec-first, a well-considered specification is written, used for the task, and then effectively discarded, and every change starts a new specification. At the second rung, spec-anchored, the specification survives the task and is maintained as the feature evolves, edited alongside the code over time. At the third rung, spec-as-source, the specification is the primary artifact, and humans edit only the specification and never touch the generated code. Every approach examined is at least spec-first, but few genuinely reach spec-anchored, and the maintenance strategy over time is usually left vague. A working definition is worth memorizing. A specification is a structured, behavior-oriented artifact, written in natural language, that expresses software functionality and serves as guidance to coding agents. Crucially, separate the specification, which is task-scoped and only relevant to the change it drives, from the memory bank, which is the cross-session rules and the product and architecture context relevant to every session. Conflating the two is why so many setups feel bloated. The honest warning attached to the top of the ladder is the model-driven development parallel. Spec-as-source is model-driven development with a natural-language model and a code generator, and model-driven development never took hold for business applications because the abstraction level was awkward and the overhead was high. Removing the parseable grammar only trades that overhead for non-determinism, risking inflexibility and unpredictability at once.

chapters.title: When This Is Too Much
chapters.script: A balanced engineer holds both truths. Spec-first is genuinely valuable, and the elaborate end of spec-driven development can make things worse while trying to make them better. The field reports are the cautionary data. The first failure is a problem-size mismatch. Asked to fix a small bug, one tool inflated it into four user stories and sixteen acceptance criteria, a sledgehammer to crack a nut, and a small feature in another produced so many files to review that the engineer felt she would have shipped it faster with plain assisted coding and stayed more in control. The second failure is review burden, verbose and repetitive prose that is more tedious to review than the code it describes. An effective tool needs a great specification-review experience, not just generation. The third failure is a false sense of control. Bigger context windows do not mean the agent honors everything in them. It regenerated existing classes as duplicates by ignoring notes that said this already exists, and elsewhere it over-applied a constitution rule too zealously. The decision is therefore not whether to adopt spec-driven development, but how to match ceremony to the problem. Small or well-understood changes favor tight iterative loops with a small blast radius. Large and well-specified work is where heavyweight spec-driven development pays for its overhead. And because agents interpret specifications non-deterministically, the validation scorecard is not optional decoration. It is the evaluation harness that tells you the amplification matched intent. The engineering value is not the label but the judgment of when a durable, right-sized specification beats a fast, disposable one.
